content: 1. The Ministry of Finance and the National Statistics Office maintain records that can serve as potential data sources for health workforce expenditure analysis. Additional references include OECD reports from 2011 and 2016, as well as WHO publications from 2007 and 2015. 2. Total expenditure on the health workforce includes all incoming financial support received from official development assistance. This encompasses scholarships, grants, wages, salaries, training, and social protection for health workers. The data is reported annually and can be sourced from the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Finance, and National Statistical Office records. 3. Total expenditure on the compensation of health workers is defined as the total amount spent on wages, salaries, and other forms of remuneration for health workers, disaggregated by healthcare financing schemes. Data sources include payroll data, income tax data, and surveys of health workers. 4. Public expenditure on the compensation of health workers refers to the total amount spent by the public sector on wages, salaries, social contributions, and other employee-related costs. This data is reported annually and can be sourced from ministries, payroll systems, and tax records. 5. Average entry-level wages and salaries for health workers exclude social contributions and are disaggregated by occupation and facility ownership (public vs. private). This data helps distinguish wage differences across sectors and is reported annually. 6. National or subnational policies on public sector wage ceilings are assessed to determine their existence and applicability. These policies often extend beyond the health sector to the entire public sector. Data is reported every three years and sourced from employment laws and policies. 7. The gender wage gap is calculated as the difference between the median earnings of men and women relative to the median earnings of men. This indicator applies to full-time employees and self-employed individuals and is reported annually. 8. The percentage of the health workforce working in hospitals is calculated by dividing the total number of health workers in hospitals by the total number of active health workers. This data is reported annually and sourced from national labor force surveys and health workforce registries. 9. The percentage of the health workforce working in residential long-term care facilities is determined by dividing the total number of health workers in such facilities by the total number of active health workers. This excludes social care workers and is reported annually. 10. The percentage of the health workforce working in ambulatory health care (primary health care level facilities) is calculated by dividing the total number of health workers in these facilities by the total number of active health workers. Ambulatory care includes outpatient services such as diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation. 11. The density of specialist surgical workers per 100,000 population is calculated by dividing the total number of specialist surgical workers (e.g., surgeons, obstetricians, anesthesiologists) by the total population. This data is reported annually and sourced from national medical specialist registries. 12. The density of family medicine practitioners per 100,000 population is calculated by dividing the total number of family medicine practitioners by the total population. These practitioners provide person-centered, continuous, and comprehensive care to individuals and families in their communities. 13. The existence of advanced nursing roles is assessed based on whether there are commonly accepted definitions of nurse practitioners and other advanced nursing roles. This includes evaluating training methods and the capacity to employ nurses in advanced roles. 14. The availability of human resources to implement the International Health Regulations (IHR) is assessed by evaluating the capacity to train and deploy multidisciplinary personnel. This includes the presence of field epidemiology training programs (FETPs) at various levels (basic, intermediate, advanced) and the ability to sustain such programs. 15. The existence of an applied epidemiology training program is evaluated based on the level of capacity established within the country. This ranges from no capacity to sustainable capacity, with programs potentially hosted domestically or through agreements with other countries.
